claim: Transposable elements comprise more than 40% of most extant mammalian genomes.
source: Transposable elements comprise more than 40% of most extant mammalian genomes (Lander et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lander et al., 2001.

claim: Certain types of transposable elements called retroelements, including short/long interspersed elements (SINEs/LINEs) and hominoid-specific retrotransposons SINE-VNTR-Alus (SVA) are active in humans and can be transposed.
source: Among these, certain types of transposable elements called retroelements, including short/long interspersed elements (SINEs/LINEs) and hominoid-specific retrotransposons SINE-VNTR-Alus (SVA) are active in humans and can be transposed (Huang et al., 2012; Maksakova et al., 2013; Ostertag et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2012; Maksakova et al., 2013; Ostertag et al., 2003.

claim: Retrotransposons cause genome instability, insertional mutagenesis, or transcriptional perturbation and are often deleterious to host species.
source: As retrotransposons cause genome instability, insertional mutagenesis, or transcriptional perturbation and are often deleterious to host species (O'Donnell and Burns, 2010), multiple defense mechanisms have evolved against transposition.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Donnell and Burns, 2010.

claim: The first line of defense against transposition is transcriptional silencing of integrated retroelements by chromatin modifications, such as DNA methylation and histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9) methylation.
source: The first line of defense is transcriptional silencing of integrated retroelements by chromatin modifications, such as DNA methylation and histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9) methylation (Fukuda and Shinkai, 2020; Goodier, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fukuda and Shinkai, 2020; Goodier, 2016.

claim: Most retroelement families are bound by Krüppel-associated box domain zinc finger proteins (KRAB-ZFPs), which coevolved to recognize specific retroelement families.
source: Most retroelement families are bound by Krüppel-associated box domain zinc finger proteins (KRAB-ZFPs), which coevolved to recognize specific retroelement families (Imbeault et al., 2017; Jacobs et al., 2014; Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Imbeault et al., 2017; Jacobs et al., 2014; Wolf et al., 2015.

claim: KRAB-ZFPs repress retroelements by recruiting KAP1/TRIM28 and other repressive epigenetic modifiers.
source: KRAB-ZFPs repress retroelements by recruiting KAP1/TRIM28 (Sripathy et al., 2006) and other repressive epigenetic modifiers (Schultz et al., 2002; Schultz et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sripathy et al., 2006; Schultz et al., 2002; Schultz et al., 2001.

claim: During embryonic development, primordial germ cells (PGCs) undergo epigenetic reprogramming, characterized by DNA demethylation and global resetting of histone marks in mice and humans.
source: During embryonic development, primordial germ cells (PGCs) undergo epigenetic reprogramming, characterized by DNA demethylation and global resetting of histone marks in mice and humans (Gkountela et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Seisenberger et al., 2012; Seki et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gkountela et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Seisenberger et al., 2012; Seki et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2015.

claim: A subset of young retroelements resists global DNA demethylation in PGCs, which may be required for retroelement silencing.
source: A subset of young retroelements resists this global DNA demethylation event in PGCs, which may be required for retroelement silencing (Gkountela et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Seisenberger et al., 2012; Seki et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gkountela et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Seisenberger et al., 2012; Seki et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2015.

claim: H3K9 trimethylation mediated by SETDB1 is enriched in DNA demethylation-resistant retroelements in mouse PGCs.
source: H3K9 trimethylation mediated by SETDB1 is enriched in DNA demethylation-resistant retroelements in mouse PGCs (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: SETDB1 regulates DNA methylation of a subset of retroelements.
source: As SETDB1 regulates DNA methylation of a subset of retroelements (Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2013), and it is recruited to the retroelements via interaction with KRAB-ZFPs, it has been hypothesized that SETDB1/KRAB-ZFPs may contribute to DNA demethylation resistance in PGCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2013.

claim: SETDB1 is recruited to retroelements via interaction with KRAB-ZFPs.
source: As SETDB1 regulates DNA methylation of a subset of retroelements (Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2013), and it is recruited to the retroelements via interaction with KRAB-ZFPs, it has been hypothesized that SETDB1/KRAB-ZFPs may contribute to DNA demethylation resistance in PGCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the context of the sentence and established knowledge about SETDB1 and KRAB-ZFPs.

claim: SETDB1/KRAB-ZFPs may contribute to DNA demethylation resistance in PGCs.
source: As SETDB1 regulates DNA methylation of a subset of retroelements (Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2013), and it is recruited to the retroelements via interaction with KRAB-ZFPs, it has been hypothesized that SETDB1/KRAB-ZFPs may contribute to DNA demethylation resistance in PGCs.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis based on inference from the cited studies.

claim: The genomic DNA of sperm is highly methylated in both humans and mice.
source: In contrast to the extensive DNA hypomethylation in PGCs, the genomic DNA of sperm is highly methylated in both humans and mice (Hammoud et al., 2014; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Molaro et al., 2011; Okae et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hammoud et al., 2014; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Molaro et al., 2011; Okae et al., 2014.

claim: Retroelements are subjected to de novo DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in mice via the PIWI/piRNA pathway.
source: Retroelements are also subjected to de novo DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in mice via the PIWI/piRNA pathway (Aravin et al., 2008; Inoue et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aravin et al., 2008; Inoue et al., 2017.

claim: Epigenetic alterations in retroelements and dysfunction of retroelement silencing pathways in male germ cells are associated with male sterility linked to azoospermia.
source: Epigenetic alterations in retroelements and dysfunction of retroelement silencing pathways in male germ cells are associated with male sterility linked to azoospermia (Aravin et al., 2007; Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004; Carmell et al., 2007; Heyn et al., 2012; Urdinguio et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aravin et al., 2007; Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004; Carmell et al., 2007; Heyn et al., 2012; Urdinguio et al., 2015.

claim: Epigenetic alterations of retroelements in male germ cells can be potentially transmitted to the next generation with phenotypic consequences.
source: In addition, epigenetic alterations of retroelements in male germ cells can be potentially transmitted to the next generation with phenotypic consequences (Daxinger et al., 2016; Rakyan et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Daxinger et al., 2016; Rakyan et al., 2003.

claim: Global erasure of DNA methylation is mostly complete at 19 weeks of gestation in male hPGCs.
source: The global erasure of DNA methylation is mostly complete at 19 weeks of gestation (Figure 1A), therefore, we analyzed the DNA methylation status of full-length transposable elements (a copy whose length is 90% or more of the length of the consensus sequence of each subtype, listed in Supplementary file 1) in male hPGCs at 19 weeks of gestation to identify retroelements that showed resistance to demethylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The primate-specific retroelement families L1PA, SVA, and LTR12 showed high levels of DNA methylation in male hPGCs at 19 weeks of gestation.
source: Among the retroelements we analyzed, the primate-specific retroelement families L1PA, SVA, and LTR12 showed high levels of DNA methylation (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the SVA family, SVA_A, which emerged 13–14 million years ago (Mya) and is the oldest SVA type, showed the highest DNA methylation levels relative to other SVA types.
source: In the SVA family, SVA_A, which emerged 13–14 million years ago (Mya) and is the oldest SVA type, showed the highest DNA methylation levels relative to other SVA types. This includes the currently active SVA_E/F (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the L1 family, L1PA3–5, which emerged 12–20 Mya and is moderately young, showed higher methylation levels than the older (L1PA5–8) and younger L1 types, including the currently active L1 (L1HS).
source: In the L1 family, L1PA3–5, which emerged 12–20 Mya and is moderately young, showed higher methylation levels than the older (L1PA5–8) and younger L1 types, including the currently active L1 (L1HS) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LTR12 (also known as HERV9 LTR) is not currently active and all LTR12 types are highly methylated.
source: LTR12 (also known as HERV9 LTR) is not currently active and all LTR12 types are highly methylated (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Young but inactive L1PA, SVA, and LTR12 types are resistant to DNA demethylation in hPGCs.
source: Therefore, it appears that young but inactive L1PA, SVA, and LTR12 types are resistant to DNA demethylation in hPGCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data presented in Figures 1C-E.

claim: 100 bp short-read NGS data did not map efficiently onto the currently active L1 transposon, L1HS.
source: Because 100 bp short-read NGS data did not map efficiently onto the currently active L1 transposon, L1HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and DNA methylation of only about 10% of full-length L1HS copies could be analyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), it is possible that a subset of L1HS is resistant to DNA demethylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNA methylation of only about 10% of full-length L1HS copies could be analyzed.
source: Because 100 bp short-read NGS data did not map efficiently onto the currently active L1 transposon, L1HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and DNA methylation of only about 10% of full-length L1HS copies could be analyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), it is possible that a subset of L1HS is resistant to DNA demethylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: It is possible that a subset of L1HS is resistant to DNA demethylation.
source: Because 100 bp short-read NGS data did not map efficiently onto the currently active L1 transposon, L1HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and DNA methylation of only about 10% of full-length L1HS copies could be analyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), it is possible that a subset of L1HS is resistant to DNA demethylation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the limitations of the data.

claim: The DNA methylation levels of each retroelement type were highly variable among full-length copies.
source: Even though some retroelement types showed relatively high DNA methylation levels in hPGCs, the DNA methylation levels of each retroelement type were highly variable among full-length copies (Figure 1C–E), which prompted us to try to identify potential DNA sequences required for DNA demethylation resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1C-E.

claim: Both the 'high' and 'low' classes of copies exist in highly methylated retroelement types in hPGCs, such as SVA_A, L1PA3, and LTR12C.
source: Using this classification, we determined that both the 'high' and 'low' classes of copies exist in highly methylated retroelement types in hPGCs, such as SVA_A, L1PA3, and LTR12C (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1F-H.

claim: ZNF257 and ZNF28 peaks overlapped more frequently with highly methylated SVA_A copies than with lowly methylated copies.
source: We observed that the ZNF257 and ZNF28 peaks overlapped more frequently with highly methylated SVA_A copies than with lowly methylated copies (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Peaks of ZNF611 and ZNF91, which interact with SVAs in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), were observed in both lowly and highly methylated SVA_A copies.
source: Because peaks of ZNF611 and ZNF91, which interact with SVAs in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Haring et al., 2021; Jacobs et al., 2014), were observed in both lowly and highly methylated SVA_A copies (Figure 2A), it is unlikely that these two KRAB-ZNPs contribute to the differences in DNA methylation among SVA_A copies.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and citations to Haring et al., 2021; Jacobs et al., 2014.

claim: It is unlikely that ZNF611 and ZNF91 contribute to the differences in DNA methylation among SVA_A copies.
source: Because peaks of ZNF611 and ZNF91, which interact with SVAs in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Haring et al., 2021; Jacobs et al., 2014), were observed in both lowly and highly methylated SVA_A copies (Figure 2A), it is unlikely that these two KRAB-ZNPs contribute to the differences in DNA methylation among SVA_A copies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Of the 'high' SVA_A elements, 63.8% and 44.7% were bound by ZNF257 or ZNF28, respectively.
source: Of the 'high' SVA_A elements, 63.8% and 44.7% were bound by ZNF257 or ZNF28, respectively. However, no 'low' SVA_A showed binding (Figure 2A), and both 'high' and 'medium' SVA_A copies significantly overlapped with the ZNF257- or ZNF28-binding peaks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No 'low' SVA_A showed binding to ZNF257 or ZNF28.
source: Of the 'high' SVA_A elements, 63.8% and 44.7% were bound by ZNF257 or ZNF28, respectively. However, no 'low' SVA_A showed binding (Figure 2A), and both 'high' and 'medium' SVA_A copies significantly overlapped with the ZNF257- or ZNF28-binding peaks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both 'high' and 'medium' SVA_A copies significantly overlapped with the ZNF257- or ZNF28-binding peaks.
source: Of the 'high' SVA_A elements, 63.8% and 44.7% were bound by ZNF257 or ZNF28, respectively. However, no 'low' SVA_A showed binding (Figure 2A), and both 'high' and 'medium' SVA_A copies significantly overlapped with the ZNF257- or ZNF28-binding peaks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The frequency of overlap with the ZNF257/28 peaks and the enrichment of ZNF257/28 in SVA_A were positively correlated with DNA methylation.
source: The frequency of overlap with the ZNF257/28 peaks and the enrichment of ZNF257/28 in SVA_A were positively correlated with DNA methylation (Figure 2B and C), and both ZNF257 and ZNF28 showed the highest enrichment of SVA_A when SVA family members were compared (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and C.

claim: Both ZNF257 and ZNF28 showed the highest enrichment of SVA_A when SVA family members were compared.
source: The frequency of overlap with the ZNF257/28 peaks and the enrichment of ZNF257/28 in SVA_A were positively correlated with DNA methylation (Figure 2B and C), and both ZNF257 and ZNF28 showed the highest enrichment of SVA_A when SVA family members were compared (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both ZNF257 and ZNF28 were expressed more in hPGCs than in neighboring somatic cells.
source: Reanalysis of single-cell RNA-seq data for hPGCs and neighboring somatic cells (Guo et al., 2015) showed that both ZNF649 and ZNF93 were expressed more in hPGCs than in neighboring somatic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B and citation to Guo et al., 2015.

claim: The ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs are in VNTR1.
source: The ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs, which were predicted by HOMER (Heinz et al., 2010; Figure 2F), are in VNTR1 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2E and 2F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within SVAs was the highest in SVA_A.
source: The number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within SVAs was the highest in SVA_A (Figure 2E) and was most strongly correlated with the copy number of VNTR1 in SVA_A out of all the SVA classes (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within SVAs was most strongly correlated with the copy number of VNTR1 in SVA_A out of all the SVA classes.
source: The number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within SVAs was the highest in SVA_A (Figure 2E) and was most strongly correlated with the copy number of VNTR1 in SVA_A out of all the SVA classes (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The VNTR1 copy number was highly variable among SVA_A copies.
source: The VNTR1 copy number was also highly variable among SVA_A copies (Figure 2G), and DNA methylation of SVA_A was positively correlated with the VNTR1 copy number (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and the number of ZNF257/28 motifs (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: DNA methylation of SVA_A was positively correlated with the VNTR1 copy number.
source: The VNTR1 copy number was also highly variable among SVA_A copies (Figure 2G), and DNA methylation of SVA_A was positively correlated with the VNTR1 copy number (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and the number of ZNF257/28 motifs (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DNA methylation of SVA_A was positively correlated with the number of ZNF257/28 motifs.
source: The VNTR1 copy number was also highly variable among SVA_A copies (Figure 2G), and DNA methylation of SVA_A was positively correlated with the VNTR1 copy number (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and the number of ZNF257/28 motifs (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: DNA methylation levels within the VNTR were correlated with ZNF257 or ZNF28 association.
source: We also confirmed that DNA methylation levels within the VNTR were correlated with ZNF257 or ZNF28 association (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: A high number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within the VNTR increases the enrichment of KRAB-ZFPs.
source: These results indicate that a high number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within the VNTR increases the enrichment of KRAB-ZFPs. This might contribute to maintaining SVA_A DNA methylation during hPGC development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data presented in Figures 2H, 2I, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: A high number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within the VNTR might contribute to maintaining SVA_A DNA methylation during hPGC development.
source: These results indicate that a high number of ZNF257- and ZNF28-binding motifs within the VNTR increases the enrichment of KRAB-ZFPs. This might contribute to maintaining SVA_A DNA methylation during hPGC development.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the correlation observed in the data.

claim: ZNF649 and ZNF93 peaks were frequently found in L1PA2–6 and L1PA3–6, respectively.
source: Consistent with previous reports that ZNF649 and ZNF93 bind L1s (Cosby et al., 2019; Jacobs et al., 2014), ZNF649 and ZNF93 peaks were frequently found in L1PA2–6 and L1PA3–6, respectively (Figure 3A), and these two KRAB-ZFPs were enriched at the 5ʹ terminus of the L1 sequences (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citations to Cosby et al., 2019; Jacobs et al., 2014.

claim: ZNF649 and ZNF93 were enriched at the 5ʹ terminus of the L1 sequences.
source: Consistent with previous reports that ZNF649 and ZNF93 bind L1s (Cosby et al., 2019; Jacobs et al., 2014), ZNF649 and ZNF93 peaks were frequently found in L1PA2–6 and L1PA3–6, respectively (Figure 3A), and these two KRAB-ZFPs were enriched at the 5ʹ terminus of the L1 sequences (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The frequency of L1 copies overlapping with ZNF649 and ZNF93 peaks was correlated with the DNA methylation levels of L1s in hPGCs.
source: The frequency of L1 copies overlapping with ZNF649 and ZNF93 peaks was correlated with the DNA methylation levels of L1s in hPGCs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Read mappability in L1 (L1PA4) was similar across the different DNA methylation groups.
source: Because read mappability in L1 (L1PA4) was similar across the different DNA methylation groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), ZNF649 and ZNF93 are candidate factors for the DNA demethylation resistance of these L1s.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ZNF649 and ZNF93 are candidate factors for the DNA demethylation resistance of L1s.
source: Because read mappability in L1 (L1PA4) was similar across the different DNA methylation groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), ZNF649 and ZNF93 are candidate factors for the DNA demethylation resistance of these L1s.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The presence of ZNF649- or ZNF93-binding motifs was correlated with DNA methylation levels of L1s.
source: As was the case for SVA_A, the presence of ZNF649- or ZNF93-binding motifs (Figure 3D) was also correlated with DNA methylation levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Both ZNF649 and ZNF93 were expressed more in hPGCs than in neighboring somatic cells.
source: Reanalysis of single-cell RNA-seq data for hPGCs and neighboring somatic cells (Guo et al., 2015) showed that both ZNF649 and ZNF93 were expressed more in hPGCs than in neighboring somatic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B and citation to Guo et al., 2015.

claim: The ZNF649-binding motif was located at the 5ʹ UTR of L1s.
source: The ZNF649-binding motif was located at the 5ʹ UTR of L1s (Figure 3F), consistent with the enrichment of ZNF649 in the 5′ UTR (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The enrichment of ZNF649 in L1s was decreased in L1PA2 and abrogated in L1HS.
source: The enrichment of ZNF649 in L1s was decreased in L1PA2 and abrogated in L1HS (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A base substitution at the fifth position of the ZNF649-binding site was observed in the consensus sequences of L1HS.
source: Along with the decreased ZNF649 enrichment, a base substitution at the fifth position of the ZNF649-binding site was observed in the consensus sequences of L1HS (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The fifth position of the ZNF649-binding site (T) is conserved in highly methylated L1 copies.
source: Because the fifth position of the ZNF649-binding site (T) is conserved in highly methylated L1 copies (Figure 3G), a T in this position may be required for ZNF649 to bind to L1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A T in the fifth position of the ZNF649-binding site may be required for ZNF649 to bind to L1.
source: Because the fifth position of the ZNF649-binding site (T) is conserved in highly methylated L1 copies (Figure 3G), a T in this position may be required for ZNF649 to bind to L1.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the conservation observed in the data.

claim: ZNF850 more frequently overlapped with highly methylated LTR12C/D/E copies than lowly methylated ones.
source: For the LTR12C family, we found that ZNF850 more frequently overlapped with highly methylated LTR12C/D/E copies than lowly methylated ones when we analyzed the binding peak data for 250 KRAB-ZFPs (Helleboid et al., 2019; Imbeault et al., 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B and citations to Helleboid et al., 2019; Imbeault et al., 2017.

claim: The ZNF850-binding motif was more frequently found in highly methylated LTR12C copies than in lowly methylated copies.
source: The ZNF850-binding motif was more frequently found in highly methylated LTR12C copies than in lowly methylated copies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Two high-confidence binding motifs (q-value < 0.01) were identified at the 5′ portion of LTR12C consensus sequences.
source: Two high-confidence binding motifs (q-value < 0.01) were identified at the 5′ portion of LTR12C consensus sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), which was consistent with ZNF850 enrichment in the 5′ portion of LTR12C (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: ZNF850 enrichment was in the 5′ portion of LTR12C.
source: Two high-confidence binding motifs (q-value < 0.01) were identified at the 5′ portion of LTR12C consensus sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), which was consistent with ZNF850 enrichment in the 5′ portion of LTR12C (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Lowly methylated LTR12C copies contained mismatches more frequently at the eighth and tenth positions of the first and second predicted binding sites along LTR12C, respectively.
source: Lowly methylated LTR12C copies contained mismatches more frequently at the eighth and tenth positions of the first and second predicted binding sites along LTR12C, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: KRAB-ZNFs prevent DNA demethylation during male germ-cell development.
source: These data suggest that KRAB-ZNFs prevent DNA demethylation during male germ-cell development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data presented in Figures 2 and 3 and their supplements.

claim: The dynamics of DNA methylation in retroelements during spermatogenesis vary depending on retroelement type and individual characteristics.
source: The dynamics of DNA methylation in retroelements during spermatogenesis vary depending on retroelement type and individual characteristics.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Most L1 copies acquired DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in both individuals.
source: Most L1 copies acquired DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in both individuals, whereas LTR12C copies maintained their DNA methylation status in hPGCs during spermatogenesis (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LTR12C copies maintained their DNA methylation status in hPGCs during spermatogenesis.
source: Most L1 copies acquired DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in both individuals, whereas LTR12C copies maintained their DNA methylation status in hPGCs during spermatogenesis (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A substantial difference between individuals was observed in the SVAs.
source: A substantial difference between individuals was observed in the SVAs. The majority of SVA copies acquired DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in sperm donor 1, but not in donor 2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of SVA copies acquired DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in sperm donor 1, but not in donor 2.
source: A substantial difference between individuals was observed in the SVAs. The majority of SVA copies acquired DNA methylation during spermatogenesis in sperm donor 1, but not in donor 2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of lowly methylated L1 copies in hPGCs were highly methylated in sperm cells from both donors.
source: The majority of lowly methylated L1 copies in hPGCs were highly methylated in sperm cells from both donors (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most LTR12C/D copies maintained their PGC DNA methylation status during spermatogenesis.
source: In contrast, most LTR12C/D copies maintained their PGC DNA methylation status during spermatogenesis (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Among the SVA types, SVA_A showed high levels of DNA methylation in both sperm donors.
source: Among the SVA types, SVA_A showed high levels of DNA methylation in both sperm donors, whereas other SVA types showed variable DNA methylation levels when both sperm donors were compared (Figure 4D), especially in SVA copies that had low DNA methylation levels in hPGCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Other SVA types showed variable DNA methylation levels when both sperm donors were compared, especially in SVA copies that had low DNA methylation levels in hPGCs.
source: Among the SVA types, SVA_A showed high levels of DNA methylation in both sperm donors, whereas other SVA types showed variable DNA methylation levels when both sperm donors were compared (Figure 4D), especially in SVA copies that had low DNA methylation levels in hPGCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.
